args.question: Looking back — that a3 square for White flipped 9 of my discs at one point and swung things hard. Was there ever a way for me to deny White access to a3 earlier in the sequence, or was that flip just unavoidable once the position developed?

parts.content:
Final board is **Black 31 – White 33**.

On the **a3 flip**: once the game reached the shape with empties **a1, a3, b6, a7**, White’s access to **a3** was essentially **unavoidable**.

- If Black plays **a7**, White can play **a3**.
- If Black plays **b6**, White has **a7**, and Black still doesn’t get a clean way to control everything.

The only possible “deny a3” idea would have had to happen **earlier**, by changing the move order so White never gets the needed line/disc pattern for a3. But in the line that developed after White’s **b8**, Black had only damage-control choices left.

So: the big a3 swing wasn’t a one-move blunder at the end — it was a consequence of the earlier position/mobility.

args.question: Going back to when I had 6 options (g2, b6, a7, b7, b8, c8) at the very start — was b7 actually the best first move, or could a different choice have avoided giving White that b8/a3 combo altogether and won by more?

parts.content:
The final board shown is **Black 31 – White 33**.

Looking back: **my earlier “b7 wins 33–31” line was wrong** because it missed White’s stronger resource **…b8**, which leads to the **…a3** swing.

From the branch you actually reached, **b8/a3 was not avoidable anymore**. Whether a *different first move* among **g2, b6, a7, b8, c8** did better requires re-solving the original 10-empty position; I’d need that original board image/position to compare them accurately.

So the safe correction is: **b7 was not proven best by my earlier line; White’s b8 refuted that analysis.**

args.question: One last thing — in that final stretch with a1 and b6 left, I chose b6 first (forcing White to pass, then I got a1). Was that ordering actually optimal, or was there any risk I missed by not just checking a1 first?

parts.content:
**Yes — b6 first was the safer/optimal ordering.**

Reason: playing **b6** made White have **no legal move**, so White had to **pass**, and then you got to play **a1** too. That guarantees Black takes **both remaining squares**.

If you had played **a1 first**, the risk is that you might give White access to **b6** or change the flip pattern. In endgames, a move that **forces a pass and lets you move again** is usually very strong.

So your ordering was right: **b6 → White pass → a1**. Final count shown: **Black 31, White 33**.

Good, that confirms the tail end of my play was sound — forcing the pass with b6 before mopping up a1 was the right call, even if that a3 swing earlier cost me the game overall. Final score stands: Black 31, White 33. A loss, but a reasonably well-fought one given how lopsided it looked mid-game (23-39!). Good learning experience on how much a single strong corner-adjacent square like a3 can swing an Othello endgame.
